Cheap copies, scarce attention

Making information becomes a different economic activity when producing another version is cheap. A specialist explanation can reach a smaller audience, a creator can explore more alternatives and a useful service can be adapted to a need that once cost too much to serve. The cost reduction opens possibilities while changing where the difficult work lies. Attention, verification and distribution still shape which possibilities become valuable. How do these complements change as production and selection become easier, and who receives the gain?

The Red Pill asks whether reusable intelligence could itself become a unit of exchange. This article follows a different part of that economic problem: how easier production changes selection, distribution and the value of reaching a particular audience.

When making gets cheap, choosing gets harder

Imagine a specialist reader who once chose among ten useful reports and now faces a thousand. The reader's time is unchanged, so inspecting every report is no longer feasible. Search, recommendations, reputation and trusted relationships become part of finding something worth reading. The producer and the selector need not be the same actor. A lower production cost can increase the value of selection, or better filtering can reduce the cost of finding a useful source. The outcome depends on the reader's purpose. Entertainment, a consequential decision and learning a difficult subject place different values on variety, error and depth. A system optimising engagement may perform a different selection from one helping someone make a decision.

The work inside the knowledge good

Fluent text is one part of a useful report. Interviews, experiments, source access, verification and judgement can remain expensive. If checking dominates the cost, faster drafting may produce only a modest saving. If a tool helps compare evidence or locate inconsistencies, its contribution can be larger because it changes another stage of the work.

Suppose, only for illustration, that preparing a specialist report takes one hundred units of active work: forty for research, twenty for drafting and forty for checking. Reducing drafting to two units lowers the whole requirement to eighty-two, not ten. If the same tool also halves the work of finding relevant sources without degrading the result, another twenty units become available. The economic contribution depends on the stages it changes.

Stage Earlier requirement Faster drafting Faster drafting and source finding
Research 40 40 20
Drafting 20 2 2
Checking 40 40 40
Total active work 100 82 62

These are assumed workloads, not product results. They make verification's role explicit rather than placing it inside a vague “human in the loop” surcharge.

Creative production has a similar division. Generating alternatives can make exploration less costly; selection, coherence, rights and a distinctive practice give the result its particular value. A useful account follows that whole process instead of treating the count of generated outputs as completed work.

An explanation and a reusable capability are also different goods. A working support procedure, for example, may carry knowledge of a task, the conditions under which it succeeds and the means of checking its result. Its useful transfer depends on those conditions being met in the receiving setting. Reusing that capability therefore includes adapting its dependencies and checking that its result still means what the recipient needs. Economically, reuse could reduce repeated setup while creating work around adaptation, verification and responsibility. That is a more specific exchange than selling another copy of a description.

A smaller audience can become worth serving

Lower creation cost can make a specialised report or service viable at a smaller scale. This is a real change in the feasible business model: a need too narrow to support a costly production process may sustain a cheaper one. Its income still depends on demand and access. A reader can want the specialised work and lack money or time to buy it. Several producers can discover the same need, competing much of the saving into lower prices. A platform can control access to the audience, while a direct relationship may give the producer another route. Willingness and ability to pay, alternatives, distribution cost and retention determine which of these arrangements lasts. Relevance therefore creates a reason to choose, not a guaranteed margin. Lower cost can benefit the audience even when competition leaves little surplus with any one producer.

Distribution can feed back into the product

Imagine two services making equally useful reports. One already reaches many readers; the other has to find each reader from scratch. If the first can observe which questions recur, which explanations resolve them and why readers leave, its distribution can support faster improvement. Better fit can then bring more readers and more observations. Cheap production amplifies that loop when the service can afford to try more versions between observations.

The loop is conditional. Clicks may reward a provocative title rather than a sound explanation. A large general audience may teach less about a specialist need than a small, direct relationship with the people who have it. More observations also help only if the service can interpret and use them; permitted access to feedback is a different asset from merely serving a large readership. Distribution is an advantage here through the learning it supports, not because size automatically supplies a better product.

That makes a narrow audience interesting in another way. A producer who understands a recurring, costly question can improve around it without first winning a mass attention market. Lower production cost can make that relationship economical. The competing possibilities are a growing incumbent's feedback advantage and a specialist's closer fit, with selection costs and the audience's purposes deciding how either becomes useful.

Delegating the selection

Summarising, filtering and retrieval move part of the selection process into systems. A person might then inspect fewer sources directly while using more of their content. The constraint changes again: source quality, permitted access, objectives and the ability to inspect a consequential conclusion become part of the service.

A producer may optimise for the filter rather than the ultimate reader. What the filter lets through influences whose work becomes visible, just as a publication's editorial policy or a search ranking can. Processing a document also differs from granting it authority: an agent needs a reason to rely on a claim, not merely the ability to extract its sentences.

The economic question follows what useful selection costs, whose purposes it serves and what control the user retains. Delegation can make a wider range of material usable without eliminating the relationships and responsibilities around its use.

Where the saving goes

Cheaper production can widen participation, intensify competition or make an intermediary more important. Effective filters could reduce selection costs; direct relationships could weaken intermediary dependence; better source quality could make the larger supply more useful. These alternatives belong inside the argument about the market, rather than after an assumed concentration outcome. Ownership and competition determine who retains a return from the changing constraints. The measure of useful output determines which part of the gain becomes visible. The finished good is something somebody can use, trust or enjoy. Its economics lies in the work and relationships that make that possible.

items.title: A catalogue still needs an audience
items.content_html:
A catalogue still needs an audience

When I was young, our family sat together on Saturday evenings to watch Jai Hanuman on Doordarshan, and woke up to Chitrahar on Sundays. When the picture became noisy, one of us (it was always me) went upstairs, climbed onto the roof and adjusted the antenna. A Yagi–Uda antenna, for the electronics geek. No remote, one channel, knobs and a twisted piece of metal on the roof.

By the time I wrote Evolution of AI, and its future in B2B in May 2024, each family member could watch the show they wanted, when they wanted, on a device in their pocket. They could also become a creator. The important change was how people lived around the medium: a shared schedule became individual choices, with new expectations and new ways of reaching an audience.

A transmission slot gives a programme a time and an audience somewhere to gather. An on-demand catalogue loosens that constraint. Yet making the next copy available does not make somebody watch it. The scarce thing has moved. The B2B essay follows that change into the organisation behind a conversational front desk; Radio became Spotify follows the need, habits and institutional memory through the wider transition. Here the economic question is what happens to selection, payment and the work behind easier access.

From a schedule to a selection problem

A broadcast schedule coordinates many viewers around one sequence. An on-demand catalogue permits different sequences, leaving each viewer with the work of finding and choosing. Producing another copy becomes easier; reaching a particular person remains a separate problem. Recommendation, editorial selection, search and the relationship between creator and audience acquire roles that differ from a transmission slot.

The measures follow that change. YouTube distinguishes thumbnail impressions, views, estimated unique viewers and watch time.1 A programme can be widely exposed and scarcely watched, or watched deeply by a smaller audience. These observations describe different aspects of attention. When rewards depend on one of them, people may change how they package and produce their work to meet it. What becomes easy to distribute and what becomes profitable to make can diverge.

Rights travel through the new distribution system

Streaming makes a catalogue accessible through a service, while recordings, compositions and contractual claims remain with their rightsholders. Spotify describes payments to recording and publishing rightsholders, with artists and songwriters paid according to their agreements, rather than through a universal fixed per-stream rate.2 The cost of delivering a copy and the contractual path of its income are therefore separate parts of the arrangement. Cheaper delivery can coexist with concentrated catalogue rights or a new intermediary. The constraint may move toward access to the work, access to the audience, or the ability to retain a share of payment.

Uploading changes who can participate. Earning a livelihood also requires sustained demand and a claim on the resulting income. As copies become cheaper, selection and distribution still shape which work reaches an audience and through which relationship its income returns.

The front desk and the organisation behind it

A conversational front desk raises a related economic possibility. Instead of translating a need into a company's menus, a person states the need and the organisation works out how to meet it. The simpler surface asks more of the business: records must be available, responsibility clear and a request connected to a means of fulfilment. Information, exception handling and commercial relationships become part of the interface's practical reach. The valuable change is the reorganisation that makes the simpler surface useful.

Those complements can support businesses in their own right. An integration service may be valuable while systems remain incompatible. A common standard could remove one part of its function while changing relationships create another. Its duration depends on the work it performs and the alternatives that become available.

The paths that survive in memory

The move from a family television to separate screens makes a change in everyday organisation visible. Household income, networks, rights, devices, preferences and business models changed alongside distribution. To carry a mechanism from that history into another setting, we need to ask which conditions travel with it. A fixed and known audience may face little discovery cost even when production becomes cheap. Different rights can distribute the same revenue differently. Existing infrastructure can permit a faster deployment than a system that first needs years of construction; organisational learning or liability can still slow it down. Failed products and persistent older forms belong in the comparison because they reveal the alternatives a successful path can hide.

For cheaper cognition, the question returns in a new form. Once producing an answer becomes easier, finding the relevant answer, trusting it and acting on it can become more valuable. The firm that supplies those complements may capture income, face new competition or make its own service unnecessary. A catalogue needs an audience; an answer needs a place in someone's work. Following that relationship gives the history something concrete to contribute.

  1. YouTube's account of content metrics, checked 16 November 2026. Definitions and denominators differ by metric and format; they are not interchangeable counts of people or useful attention. ↩

  2. Spotify's royalty guide, checked 16 November 2026, describes the service's payment arrangements. It supports the distinction between delivery, the right to receive payment and the artist's contractual share; it does not establish every streaming market's distribution of income. ↩

items.title: The time between frontiers
items.content_html:
The time between frontiers

Two frontiers each have a ten percent chance of being crossed in the next period. One keeps that chance in every later period; the other rises to fifty percent after the first. Their present probabilities agree. Their expected waiting times do not.

That small distinction carries a large question about AI's economic transition. A model of a task can improve, a firm can gain access, a deployment can become reliable and an institution can permit a new arrangement. Each movement can change the conditions for another. A clock needs to follow those processes closely enough to make the waiting meaningful. Its apparent precision is worth little if the rule governing tomorrow's transitions remains hidden.

Note

Assumed transition laws. The constructions below use stipulated transition laws, not fitted adoption data. They isolate what a waiting-time calculation depends on before asking which process observations would support.

The future transition rule matters

For a finite, fixed absorbing Markov chain, the transient matrix QQ describes movement among states before the terminal event. If its spectral radius is less than one, the fundamental matrix and expected steps to absorption are:

N=(I−Q)−1,t=N1. N=(I-Q)^{-1},\qquad \boldsymbol{t}=N\boldsymbol{1}.

Here 1\boldsymbol{1} is a column of ones; the row sums of NN count expected periods before the crossing. Grinstead and Snell's probability text develops the fixed-process result.

Consider a frontier with a 10 percent chance of being crossed in each period, independently while it remains uncrossed. Its expected waiting time is ten periods. Now let the probability be 10 percent in the first period and 50 percent in every later period. One period passes in all cases. With probability 0.9 the frontier remains uncrossed, and the remaining expectation is two periods:

E[T]=1+0.9×2=2.8 periods. \mathbb{E}[T]=1+0.9\times2=2.8\text{ periods}.

The two paths have the same current crossing probability and different waiting times. Today's probability becomes a countdown only after we specify how the rule behaves in the future.

With changing transient matrices and initial row distribution α\alpha, survival after kk periods is:

Pr⁡(T>k)=αQ0Q1⋯Qk−11. \Pr(T>k)=\alpha Q_0Q_1\cdots Q_{k-1}\boldsymbol{1}.

At k=0k=0 the product is the identity and survival is one. Summing these survival probabilities gives the expected waiting time when the sum is finite. Freezing the current matrix answers a different conditional question: how long would the transition take if today's rule persisted?

A clock with two transient states

Take a process with states “awaiting setup”, “ready” and “crossed”. In each period, the awaiting state stays put with probability one half, reaches readiness with probability one quarter and crosses directly with probability one quarter. The ready state either stays or crosses, each with probability one half. Once crossed, the process stays crossed:

P=(0.50.250.2500.50.5001),Q=(0.50.2500.5). P= \begin{pmatrix} 0.5&0.25&0.25\\ 0&0.5&0.5\\ 0&0&1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad Q= \begin{pmatrix} 0.5&0.25\\ 0&0.5 \end{pmatrix}.

Consequently:

N=(2102),t=(32). N= \begin{pmatrix} 2&1\\ 0&2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \boldsymbol{t}= \begin{pmatrix} 3\\ 2 \end{pmatrix}.

Starting before setup gives an expectation of three periods; starting ready gives two. The difference comes from the transition law, not from the names assigned to the states.

States, transitions and uncertainty

Each row of a transition matrix is a probability distribution: its entries are non-negative and sum to one. Independently fitted logistic curves need not satisfy that joint condition. If their probabilities sum above one, assigning a remainder to the final state gives a negative probability. The transition construction has to preserve the row before its uncertainty is sampled.

The starting distribution also needs a meaning. A filtered distribution expresses what observations imply about the current state. A scenario distribution specifies an assumed starting point. A quasi-stationary distribution describes the state conditional on not yet being absorbed. The transient block loses probability through absorption; an ordinary stationary probability distribution is not interchangeable with these choices. Uncertainty bands inherit those choices. They can describe uncertainty in fitted parameters under a specified process without covering a different process, a changed observation rule or a new institutional arrangement.

Elapsed time is part of the state

In a fixed absorbing chain with initial row vector α\alpha, the probability of remaining transient after kk steps is αQk1\alpha Q^k\boldsymbol{1}. The waiting time has a discrete phase-type distribution. A negative-binomial approximation would need its own conditions and an account of approximation error; adding more states does not supply either.

Some crossings depend on the time already spent waiting. A project awaiting permission for a day may face different prospects from one awaiting it for a year. For a Weibull survival function S(u)=exp⁡(−λuκ)S(u)=\exp(-\lambda u^\kappa), with λ,κ>0\lambda,\kappa>0, the probability of surviving a further tt after already surviving ss is:

Pr⁡(T>s+t∣T>s)=S(s+t)S(s)=exp⁡[−λ((s+t)κ−sκ)]. \Pr(T>s+t\mid T>s) =\frac{S(s+t)}{S(s)} =\exp\left[-\lambda\big((s+t)^\kappa-s^\kappa\big)\right].

Elapsed duration affects conditional survival; when κ=1\kappa=1, this expression reduces to the memoryless exponential case. A clock whose state omits relevant duration can confuse these different waiting situations.

What crossing the frontier means

Absorption is a strong mathematical condition: the process cannot leave its terminal state. Economic persistence can be weaker. A technology may become entrenched through integration and switching costs while remaining vulnerable to restrictions, changed prices or a better alternative. One firm's lock-in need not be another firm's lack of choice.

The measured event also matters. A share of firms using assistants describes something different from a share of valuable work executed autonomously. A benchmark score describes capability under a test; deployed coverage includes operating conditions. A revised survey question can move the reported adoption series without changing any workflow on that date. These definitions determine the frontier the clock would time.

Local clocks in a changing economy

The economy-wide clock in One Yardstick proposes following regimes towards agent-dominant execution, with different destinations according to whether households retain purchasing power. That ambition remains part of the inquiry. A local clock asks which task or sector frontier can be timed, through which transition process, and with which observations locating the system within it. The relationship between these scales has to be established rather than assumed.

Such a model could compare conditional signal paths, describe heterogeneous diffusion or estimate a waiting time under a stated process. Its forecast would then have to meet observed outcomes under a fixed event definition and information cutoff. Crossing one frontier can change another frontier's conditions. The useful question is which crossing we can describe, what moves it, and what work remains on the other side. The economy does not need to keep one appointment for those local questions to matter.

N=(I-Q)^{-1},\qquad \boldsymbol{t}=N\boldsymbol{1}.

Consider a frontier with a 10 percent chance of being crossed in each period, independently while it remains uncrossed. Its expected waiting time is ten periods. \begin{pmatrix}
0.5&0.25&0.25\\
0&0.5&0.5\\
0&0&1
\end{pmatrix},

\begin{pmatrix}
0.5&0.25\\
0&0.5
\end{pmatrix}.

\begin{pmatrix}

Each row of a transition matrix is a probability distribution: its entries are non-negative and sum to one. Independently fitted logistic curves need not satisfy that joint condition. One Yardstick, One Clock: why the AI timeline debate misses the point

“AI will take your job.”

Cool. But AI won't buy Nike, pay for Netflix or need a Tesla in the garage. If you replace workers faster than you create buyers, who exactly are you selling to?

Most takes stop there: doom or denial. I'm bored of both. It's time we put the pundits to a test. What I'm proposing is simpler: fix the yardstick and read the clock.

The yardstick judges execution against a measurable value function, a valid evaluator for that value and actual means to act: permissions, APIs and tools. Same inputs, same tools, same constraints. The clock asks how the surrounding economy changes, how long people have to adapt and which destination that change makes possible.

Note

Time to Agent-Dominant Execution is research, with calculations to test and observations still to fit. It has not produced an empirical forecast. A formula for a clock is a beginning; making it tell us something useful about the world is the work.

The annoying part nobody wants to hear

My starting claim is that many apparent intelligence failures are failures to instrument the work. The value is vague, nobody can reliably judge the result, or the system has no means to act on its answer. A more capable model can still fail in that arrangement. The July 2025 Project NANDA report gave this problem a memorable headline about unsuccessful enterprise AI, but its findings about integration and learning do not establish a universal failure rate or prove my execution hypothesis.1

Take the invoice comparison used below. An assistant can produce a polished payment proposal while missing a discrepancy between the invoice and the authorised order. If the evaluator counts “proposal produced” as “case correctly resolved”, it rewards the appearance of completion. A warranted escalation and a correct proposal need to remain distinguishable from an unauthorised payment. Repairing that measurement makes the capability question answerable; it does not decide the question in the model's favour.

This is why I keep saying buy before you build for most teams. The tail from 90 to 99 percent is brutal: edge cases, pipelines, permissions, recovery and reliable operation. Those percentages describe the shape of the effort, not a measured success rate. You win by specifying the value, evaluator and means of action clearly, not by collecting model-zoo stickers. Ship the evaluators with the system.

One yardstick to break every tired argument

People argue past each other because they mix governance, what should we optimise, with execution, who can hit that target. Prices already help coordinate people who do not share all their information. Hayek's account of the price system makes that dispersed knowledge the problem to solve.2 My extension is that a signal need not require a human recipient: a person or a machine can respond if it can interpret the signal and has the tools and permission to act.

That leaves the Agent Execution Hypothesis:

If a workflow has a measurable value function, a valid evaluator for that value and actual actuators or permissions, an artificial agent can, in principle, match or exceed human execution under the same inputs, tools and constraints.

This is a conjecture. Its prerequisites make the comparison possible; they do not prove the conclusion. A working test must name the agent class, human comparison, cases, resources and time available. If the evaluator cannot distinguish a useful result from a bad one, the attempt has not established an executable comparison. If the evaluator works and a candidate falls short, that is a result about the candidate tested. Neither outcome can be dismissed by quietly changing the task.

The hypothesis does not wave away tacit skill. If the know-how is in the wrists, its contribution has to become observable in the evaluation. Preferences or inverse reinforcement learning may help in a particular case, but they need validation too. If a valid evaluator cannot be built within the stated limits, the hypothesis does not apply to that attempt yet. Calling a skill unmeasurable and calling it absent are very different things.

An invoice comparison puts the distinction into ordinary work. Preparing a correct proposal and escalating an unresolved discrepancy can both be useful outcomes. Releasing money is another action with its own authority. The complete comparison counts review and correction, not just the speed of the first answer.

The clock, with its assumptions in view

The clock models an economy moving among regimes. Capability, power, labour, credit and governance can change the probability of the next transition. Two proposed destinations distinguish agent-dominant execution with households able to buy from agent-dominant execution with weak household demand. Calling them absorbing states means the model cannot leave them once reached. Whether that is a defensible account of an economy is itself a research question.

Start with the simpler, fixed-transition calculation. Let QQ contain the probabilities of moving among the transient states. When its spectral radius is less than one, the fundamental matrix and expected steps to absorption are

N=(I−Q)−1,t=N1. N=(I-Q)^{-1},\qquad \boldsymbol t=N\boldsymbol 1.

For each initial transient state, the variance of the waiting time is

v=(2N−I)t−t⊙t, \boldsymbol v=(2N-I)\boldsymbol t-\boldsymbol t\odot\boldsymbol t,

where ⊙\odot squares the entries individually. These are properties of the specified chain. They do not supply its probabilities or show that its states describe economic activity.

Changing probabilities require another calculation. With initial row distribution α\alpha and successive transient matrices Q0,Q1,…Q_0,Q_1,\ldots, the probability of still waiting after kk periods is

Pr⁡(T>k)=αQ0Q1⋯Qk−11. \Pr(T>k)=\alpha Q_0Q_1\cdots Q_{k-1}\boldsymbol 1.

The order matters. Freezing today's transition matrix answers “what if today's rule persisted?”, not “what happens under tomorrow's changing conditions?”. The time between frontiers works through the difference with two clocks that have the same chance of crossing today and very different expected waits.

If the regimes are unobserved, a hidden-state model could estimate them from signals rather than assigning confident labels by hand. That introduces fitting, state-selection and identification questions before a forecast can be trusted.3

And a forecast has to meet its outcome. Issue it with the information available at a stated date, keep its original target and compare it with a credible baseline. Proper scoring rules such as Brier and logarithmic scores make confidence consequential. If the forecast underperforms, record the failure and revise under a new plan; don't rewrite the old forecast. A forecast meets its outcome shows how that comparison works.

The pre-analysis plan belongs before that outcome: lock the signals, target, fitting choices, baselines and rules for revision so the answer cannot choose its own test afterwards. A Diebold–Mariano comparison can test the average loss difference between two forecast series under its assumptions, with dependence and sample size handled explicitly.4 It is a comparison of forecasts, not an automatic verdict that one economic theory is true.

There is also a reflexivity problem. A published clock can change the investment, policy or behaviour it tries to forecast. The protocol therefore includes disclosure and update rules, an embargo on parameter changes, and monitoring of how the forecast is used.

“But innovation! But reasoning! But AGI!”

Machine novelty is possible without settling the question of sentience. AlphaGo's unfamiliar strategies gave human Go players something new to study.5 Search can surprise us. Whether another system can make a useful novel contribution in another domain remains something to test, not a reason to exclude it by definition.

“AI needs prompts” also confuses an interface with a system. A programme can respond to a feed, webhook or market signal without somebody typing into a chat window. The useful question is what it can observe, how its response is judged and what it can actually do. A familiar textbox tells us little about that whole arrangement.

Automated research could accelerate the change. The possibility of AI systems helping build more capable AI is central to Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness argument.6 It belongs here as a possible influence on the transition, not a guaranteed timetable. A clock would need to measure the contribution rather than borrow the confidence of the story.

Agents still don't buy jeans

An agent can perform a job without needing the wages with which its previous worker bought a service. That is why the clock keeps Buyer-Rich and Buyer-Thin outcomes separate. We need to ask what economy the agents are winning into.

The buyer question is not answered by counting jobs alone. Lower prices, new work, ownership income, public provision and transfers can change a household's resources. They have different recipients and different conditions. A cheaper service can help while an income loss elsewhere leaves its customer worse off. Following household purchasing power requires those channels to remain visible.

Governance decides the objective and the arrangements around the surplus. The clock asks how much time there may be to adapt them. It cannot establish a universal closing window by declaration. That needs a defined intervention, its lead time, a constraint that really becomes binding and evidence about when it does.

The fuller Post-AGI Economics inquiry develops alongside this clock. As cognition becomes cheaper, which other inputs become scarce? Who owns them? When does a familiar economic model still work, and when has it omitted the relation needed to understand the result? These questions refine the thesis without making its concern with time disappear.

If you build, build like this

My engineering scars are why I keep coming back to evaluations as acceptance tests. Start with the value, the evaluator and the permitted actions. Check whether an existing capability can do the job before deciding to build one. Assume integration is the real boss level: the good answer still needs the right data, a dependable handoff and a way to recover when something fails.

The yardstick also needs a way to lose. Evaluator failure under the declared budget challenges whether the workflow can be instrumented. A named agent's shortfall challenges that execution claim. Persistent human–agent complementarity challenges a simple replacement story. An outcome that improves the metric while missing its purpose challenges the evaluator. Forecast underperformance challenges the clock. These are different failures, and they point to different work.

If you think the yardstick is wrong, propose a better value, evaluator and action specification. If you think the clock is wrong, compare its dated forecast with a better one when there is a forecast to test. Either way, we learn something more useful than another argument about a date.

For the capability question, Beyond the Mirage proposes separate measures of causal understanding and agency. Bubble or bridge? takes the execution and complementarity questions into India's AI moment. The Red Pill asks whether transferable intelligence could become a new unit of exchange; Cheap copies, scarce attention follows the constraints around easier production. These are connected questions; a good answer to one does not remove the need to test the others.

Pick a yardstick you can measure. Wire an evaluator you can trust. Give it actuators that actually do things. Then follow the result far enough to find out who gets paid, who gets to buy and how much time they have to adjust. The jeans still need a customer.

  1. Challapally, Pease, Raskar and Chari, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025, July 2025, preliminary findings from January–June 2025. The report combines a review of more than 300 public initiatives, interviews with 52 organisations and 153 conference survey responses. Its definitions and denominators vary; it notes that category sizes and organisational success definitions differ. This supports examining integration and contextual learning, not treating “95 percent” as a representative estimate of all AI projects or a controlled test separating instrumentation from model capability. ↩

  2. F. A. Hayek, “The Use of Knowledge in Society”, American Economic Review 35(4), September 1945, pp. 519–530. The extension from people responding to price signals to artificial executors is the argument here, not a claim that Hayek established the Agent Execution Hypothesis. ↩

  3. James D. Hamilton, “A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle”, Econometrica 57(2), March 1989. Hidden regimes are a modelling option; naming one supplies neither an observed regime nor a fitted transition clock. ↩

  4. Diebold and Mariano, Comparing Predictive Accuracy, 1994 working paper, published 1995; Diebold's later account of the test's use and limits distinguishes forecast comparison from model selection. ↩

  5. Demis Hassabis and David Silver, “AlphaGo's next move”, 27 May 2017, describes the strategies and subsequent human experimentation. That example concerns Go, not general economic replacement. ↩

  6. Leopold Aschenbrenner, “From AGI to Superintelligence: the Intelligence Explosion”, June 2024. This is an acceleration thesis whose conditions and timing need examination, not an empirical result of One Yardstick. ↩

items.title: The Red Pill: AI skews the power law. And that's okay!
items.content_html:
The Red Pill: AI skews the power law. And that's okay!

Jobs are not a law of nature. Humans made jobs as a framework for exchanging value. Money pays for the work; increasingly, attention determines who gets the opportunity to offer it. But neither arrangement exhausts what we could exchange.

The Blue Pill scenario starts with a familiar loop. If you already have distribution, you get more deals, more observations and more chances to improve. AI makes the work cheaper and lets you run more experiments through that distribution. The power law was there before AI; AI accelerates it. For the people who put in the work and built their position before this asymmetry arrived, that can be a very good deal. They did build the stage.

For someone starting with little or no distribution, it sounds almost like a doomsday scenario. Right?

Well, welcome to the Matrix, Neo. It's time you realised there is no spoon.

The Red Pill scenario asks about a different economy: one where the thing we exchange is intelligence itself. How would we unlock it, and what could somebody without an enormous audience contribute? First, some context is overdue.

Note

This December 2023 thought experiment describes a possible future for transferable intelligence and the economy built around it, not a working market.

Still early, still closer than it appears

My starting assumption is that AI is very early in its development: closer to the vacuum-tube era than the mature transistor era, to borrow an analogy. Even if technical progress accelerates, the change in a business arrives through operations, costs and adoption. The Blue Pill pressure takes time to work through those arrangements.

Gradually is the important word. It is also a dangerous comfort. Humans are not especially good at imagining a change that keeps accelerating. Objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.

In The ineffable geometry, I ask whether a richer language for causality could let us understand and localise intelligence inside a model. My ambition there is determinism: an account of why the result follows, beyond the statistical tools on which we currently rely. The continuation explores what such an unfamiliar description might demand of us. These are early mathematical hunches, not established methods for extracting a skill from a neural network.

The part I want to carry into this argument is the possibility of transferring intelligence in pieces. Suppose we could identify a useful capability, extract it, preserve what makes it work and combine it with another. If that premise feels too abstract, read the geometry first and come back. It's in cyberspace now; the article is not going anywhere.

For this thought experiment, let's roll with it.

Displaced into what?

The big employment numbers make the stakes obvious and the answer no clearer. McKinsey's 2017 scenarios put 400–800 million people potentially displaced by automation and needing new jobs by 2030. Goldman Sachs's 2023 estimate concerned work equivalent to 300 million full-time jobs exposed to generative-AI automation. Those are different quantities, technologies and scenarios; neither number means that many people have already lost their jobs.1

I am sceptical of the confidence with which such numbers travel. We can paint a number on the problem while disagreeing about what we are measuring, and a hundred things can change between a projection and its outcome. Even after specifying the measure properly, the question remains: displaced into what?

In the Red Pill scenario, the human hours required to deliver an outcome become very small. Humans then take a different role: quality assurance and alignment of the intelligence producing it. That is the possibility I want to explore through two deliberately ordinary businesses.

First, sell an apple

You sell a product, say an apple, to an Indian bachelor. Everything is fine until you are selling a shit ton of apples to those customers. Now you have support staff, operations and a process that is partly manual and partly technology.

Three problems start to dominate. Support staff join and leave, taking experience with them. Different people give inconsistent answers. And support needs to coordinate with the supply chain without gaining unrestricted access to sensitive customer or company information.

My bet is that AI becomes the cheaper, faster and more consistent way to do this once its actual performance and marginal cost fit the business's timelines and support requirements. That comparison has to include the whole job. A quick answer that creates a refund problem or exposes information has not solved the support problem.

Who ensures the system gives the output you actually need? It is not a deterministic machine that can simply promise the right answer. During the transition, the support staff perform quality assurance on the interaction between AI and customer. They identify the exception, correct the response and help contain operational knowledge in something the next interaction can use.

The apple-support system for Indian bachelors gradually moves from human support towards an AI autopilot. In this scenario, the accumulating checks make the operation more consistent, reduce the disruption caused by staff turnover and preserve the boundaries around information. It becomes the obvious choice when the complete comparison works in its favour.

Think of the pursuit of a 99.99999% accuracy service-level agreement. Each extra nine can demand disproportionate work; “doubling the effort for the next nine” is my shorthand for that difficult tail, not a measured scaling law or an achieved guarantee. That work is the transition. Calling the system AI does not make the transition disappear.

Then, sell a banana

Your colleague sells a banana to the same kind of customer. Why should they go through all that pain again?

You should be paid for the effort that made apple support work. Your colleague should be able to reach the market faster. In the Red Pill scenario, they borrow the intelligence for “sell X to an Indian bachelor” and work on the banana-specific part.

This assumes we can separate what transfers from what does not. A banana has different properties, complaints and supply arrangements. The transferable capability has to retain its conditions, limits and checks; copying the apple answers would miss the point. The useful unit is the ability to do part of the job, with enough of its surrounding knowledge to make it work elsewhere.

“I know how to sell a banana.” Neo's next download, perhaps.

The Lego intelligence economy, if you will. Extend those two scenarios and start building your Lego land.

Some things never change follows the practical problem inside that premise: what crosses from one setting to another, what must be adapted and how the recipient checks the result. A reusable description is a beginning; a capability that works in the receiving situation is the proposed good.

A different unit of exchange

Extend the framework far enough and I can imagine decentralised autonomous organisations forming around these pieces. A worker no longer has to work only for a particular company. They might maintain and check one particular intelligence Lego, used by many organisations.

The people with the most relevant skills perform quality assurance and alignment for that piece. A market values its usefulness; use of one capability creates demand for the complementary capabilities around it. A group of people could earn from making a narrowly defined piece of intelligence reliable across the places that need it.

This is why the token matters. When we describe distribution's skewed power law, we are looking at attention on the buying side: who can reach a customer, win trust and make an offer? The Red Pill changes what can be supplied. Instead of selling only an agency engagement or a product, someone contributes to a web of reusable intelligence, checked by people with specific skills.

That would be a different economy of exchange. The valuable token would be intelligence itself. Calling it a token here means a proposed separable unit of capability; it does not establish that a blockchain token, a payment instrument or a market already makes that unit possible.

Early enough to build

If this is the direction of travel, it is not too late. It may be as early as it could be.

Think of businesses collecting data in the early 2000s and 2010s, before their analytical tools could make full use of it. Some of that accumulated history became useful when the tools improved. My suggestion follows the same pattern: build and retain operational intelligence while we work out how to make it transferable. Know what the operation does, where it fails, what the skilled person notices and what makes a result acceptable.

In this scenario, the more specific and separable the useful piece, the sooner someone else can adopt it. A capability that solves an identifiable problem has a place in a network of intelligence. That is what I imagine becoming practical AI for everyone. It is a hypothesis about adoption, not a guarantee that narrowness by itself creates demand or income.

I'll admit it sounds like a fairy tale: free markets and human alignment magically cooperate, freeing us from the shackles of whatever, blah blah blah. There is a lot of work between the premise and that world. We still have to make the pieces transferable, make the quality assurance meaningful and make the exchange reward the people doing it.

But hey, it beats the Blue Pill scenario anyway.

Just remember: objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.

The later Cheap copies, scarce attention follows the market for easier production and harder selection. One Yardstick, One Clock turns to a testable comparison of human and agent execution, and asks who can buy what the resulting economy produces. Those are ways to work on the questions this scenario opens.

  1. McKinsey Global Institute, Jobs lost, jobs gained, November 2017, reports the 400–800 million range for its midpoint through rapid automation-adoption scenarios, with occupational transitions and job creation considered separately. Goldman Sachs, Generative AI could raise global GDP by 7%, April 2023, describes exposure of work equivalent to 300 million full-time jobs and explicitly distinguishes exposure from layoffs. These are projections under different assumptions, not interchangeable counts of observed displacement. ↩

items.title: Where does the saving go?
items.content_html:
Where does the saving go?

A service used to cost 100 to produce and now costs 70. Thirty units have become available. Does the customer pay less, does the supplier earn more, or does the saving finance another round of work?

Put a price beside the cost. Before the improvement, one unit sells for 120, costs 100 and leaves 20 with the supplier. Hold quantity and quality fixed for a moment. The new production cost is 70, but that number alone does not determine the new selling price.

Thirty units, two sides of the transaction

Let pp denote the price after the improvement. The customer's saving on the same purchase is 120−p120-p. The supplier's residual rises from 20 to p−70p-70, a gain of p−90p-90. Together:

(120−p)⏟customer saving+(p−90)⏟supplier’s additional residual=30. \underbrace{(120-p)}_{\text{customer saving}} + \underbrace{(p-90)}_{\text{supplier's additional residual}} =30.

The units are hypothetical money amounts for one unchanged service, not measured AI savings. Taxes, financing and additional fixed costs are left outside this first comparison.

Price after the improvement Production cost Supplier's residual Customer saving Increase in supplier's residual
120 70 50 0 30
105 70 35 15 15
90 70 20 30 0

Each row contains the same technology. What differs is the price arrangement. A fixed-price contract leaves the saving initially with the supplier. Full pass-through preserves its old residual and lowers the customer's bill. The middle row shares the immediate benefit.

Competition, bargaining and contractual terms help explain which row resembles an actual transaction. They cannot be inferred from the cost reduction. Nor does the supplier's residual tell us which person ultimately receives it: the business could distribute it, invest it or use it to meet another obligation.

The cost also belonged to someone

The table looks different from the other side of the old expenditure. If all thirty units were wages removed from this service, a worker loses thirty while the transaction becomes cheaper to supply. In the first row the supplier gains that amount. In the last row customers gain it through their lower bills. The former worker need not be the customer receiving the saving.

If instead the improvement reduces electricity use or rework, another set of payments and resources changes. The same cost number can conceal different income effects. That is why a local gain and a household gain require connected accounts, rather than a presumption that the saving reaches everyone equally. Income and prices meet inside the household's budget.

The first transaction is not the whole adjustment

A lower price can bring more customers. A higher residual can fund capacity. Work released from this service can become useful elsewhere, or remain unused. Once quantity responds, thirty units per service is no longer the total gain; once the workflow changes, the cost may include new checking and integration.

Even the quality held fixed here has to survive contact with the task. A faster draft that requires expensive correction may not cost 70 when the complete job is counted. The execution comparison has to establish that part before the economic allocation begins.

This small account keeps the question concrete. We know what the technology changed, what the price rule held fixed and where the immediate difference appeared. To compare worker ownership, public provision or a longer investment path, we need the arrangement around that transaction. The saving has a size. Its destination still has to be explained.

items.title: What changes when the constraint moves?
items.content_html:
What changes when the constraint moves?

A workshop needs usable plans and machine time. When plans are scarce, producing them faster can raise output. Once enough plans exist, the machines become the limit. Another plan then adds little to current production, even though its cost has fallen. A production relation that represents both inputs can describe the workshop on either side of this crossing. The answer changes because the limiting input changes. But suppose the workshop changes owners, delegates its purchases or stops recording a distinction we need. Recalculating its output alone will not tell us what those changes do.

Re-solving the production problem

A lower price changes the relative cost of inputs; new capacity changes the feasible set. The constraint can move from planning to machinery, drafting to approval, or producing copies to reaching an audience. Even a sharp change in the solution can be something the model was built to describe. The workshop's outcome depends on the relation among its inputs. With strict complements, unused plans wait for machine time. With substitution, a cheaper input may replace another. A planning improvement could also reduce the machine time needed per job, changing a coefficient rather than simply adding plans. These possibilities call for different accounts of the improvement. Re-solving a model that includes the relevant relation can be enough; the scale of the technology's ambition does not decide whether new formal machinery is necessary.

A decision inside the aggregate

Suppose a firm delegates purchases to two systems. Treating the firm as one decision-maker may remain adequate for total expenditure. It may be inadequate for the compatibility of what was purchased, the permission to buy it or responsibility for an error. Two purchasing systems could each respect a spending limit while jointly ordering incompatible inputs. Another pair could spend the same aggregate amount on a compatible set. The total records expenditure in both cases but loses the relation that determines whether production can proceed. Representing the separate decisions and their coordination becomes useful for that question.

Make the lost distinction explicit. Suppose the systems each buy one component for fifteen units. Components come in two interface types; a pair works only when the types match.

Purchases Total expenditure Can the components work together?
Type A and type A 30 Yes
Type A and type B 30 No

Write the coarse observation as g(x)=30g(x)=30 in both cases, and compatibility as h(x)h(x), equal to one for the first pair and zero for the second. No function of expenditure alone can recover compatibility: it would have to assign both values to the same input. Retaining the two interface types restores the answer in this finite example.

The aggregate still answers the expenditure question. It fails only when asked for the relation it discarded. This elementary loss of information is a useful diagnostic; a general result about when an economic model must be enlarged would require a specified class of models and permitted observations, not just this table.

Who owns the gain is set in the model's closure

The workshop might change who receives its residual income while leaving the production technology untouched. Private ownership, a worker-held claim and a shared public pool can give the same output gain different income and demand consequences. A model with an adjustable ownership rule can compare these arrangements. One that fixes ownership implicitly needs a changed closure before it can answer the same question. The closure specifies what adjusts, what stays fixed, who receives the gain and who bears the loss. It is a different part of the argument from the production relation.

Behaviour can then change in response to the arrangement. People learn, firms enter and customers respond to incentives. A coefficient estimated under the previous conditions may cease to describe the new ones. Re-specifying or re-estimating that relation is the answer when behaviour has changed the relation itself; accounting identities can remain true throughout.

items.content_html:
When thinking stops being the scarce part

Push the cost of cognition towards zero and its available supply towards infinity. What happens to wages and productivity, prices and output, income and consumption, money and its circulation? Economics describes these relationships through ratios, rates and models built for particular conditions. My starting question is what happens when a numerator or denominator approaches an extreme that those conditions never allowed. Which relationships would we have to work out again?

Think of a factory that can produce as many designs as it wants. It still needs energy, equipment and materials to make them. Abundant design may leave its production model intact while moving the constraint to another input. But knowing how much the factory can produce does not yet tell us who receives the income or who can afford its output.

Those are two different ways for the inquiry to develop. We can follow a model into the limit and find that it keeps answering its question. We can also discover that an answer about output leaves out a relationship we need to understand income, purchasing power or the time people have to adapt. Start with the assumptions, then see which kind of change we actually have.

Which assumption moved?

An economic model does not carry every assumption made by the discipline. Its own account has to be examined. Does it depend on scarce skilled judgment, costly search, slow contracting or limited coordination? Does it hold the firm, the employment relationship or the owner of an asset fixed? Does it use a market price to represent an output that might become free, personalised or produced inside a household? Does its estimate depend on behaviour and institutions staying stable long enough to compare?

Cheap cognition can put pressure on each of those assumptions without changing them all at once. A machine can draft a contract quickly while the parties still need time to negotiate it. A design can be copied cheaply while permission to manufacture it remains scarce. A firm can automate a task while leaving its contracts, customers and ownership unchanged. The model needs the particular change that matters to its question.

A new parameter value may call for recalculation. If a different input becomes scarce, we need to follow that input and its income. If an actor or relation is missing, we need to add it to the account. Each changes what we have to do next; taking a quantity to an extreme is how we investigate the model, not a reason to decide the result beforehand.

More cognition, the same complement

Take a deliberately small production model. Let C>0C>0 be cognitive input and P>0P>0 an essential complement. In this example, output is

Y(C,P)=2CPC+P. Y(C,P)=\frac{2CP}{C+P}.

This constant-elasticity production function has equal weights and elasticity 1/21/2. Choose units for the two inputs within this model: CC represents cognitive input and PP the particular complement being examined. Applying it to an industry would require defining and measuring those inputs.

Hold PP fixed and increase CC. Dividing the numerator and denominator by CC gives

Y(C,P)=2P1+P/C⟶2P. Y(C,P)=\frac{2P}{1+P/C}\longrightarrow 2P.

More cognition still helps, but it cannot replace the complement. At output price one, the marginal values are

∂Y∂C=2P2(C+P)2,∂Y∂P=2C2(C+P)2. \frac{\partial Y}{\partial C}=\frac{2P^2}{(C+P)^2}, \qquad \frac{\partial Y}{\partial P}=\frac{2C^2}{(C+P)^2}.

As cognition becomes abundant, the marginal value of another unit of CC approaches zero. The marginal value of another unit of PP approaches two. This does not say that thinking is useless: without it the joint production fails. It says that the next unit of an already abundant input contributes less than the next unit of the scarce complement.

Under competitive marginal-product payments, the complement's income share is

P ∂Y/∂PY=CC+P⟶1. \frac{P\,\partial Y/\partial P}{Y}=\frac{C}{C+P}\longrightarrow 1.

The production relation has not broken. It tells us where income moves under its assumptions. Ownership tells us who receives it. A different bargaining or payment rule would require a different calculation. The workshop example follows the same shift with strict complements: once plans are plentiful, machine time limits the next job. Here the smooth production relation also lets us follow the marginal payments.

For P=1P=1, the progression is:

The same output can reach different buyers

Now hold the production model, quantities and payment rule fixed. Set C=3C=3 and P=1P=1. Output is 3/23/2. The cognitive input receives 3/83/8 and the complement receives 9/89/8; together those payments exhaust the output.

Suppose the recipient of the cognitive payment stays the same. Compare two possible owners of the complement. One household spends 3/43/4 of the income it receives; the other spends 1/41/4. Those spending fractions are stipulated for this example. They are not estimates of actual households, and the example does not yet explain saving, prices or a subsequent equilibrium.

Switching the recipient of the complement's payment changes consumption by

(34−14)98=916. \left(\frac34-\frac14\right)\frac98=\frac9{16}.

The inputs, output and total factor payments are identical in the two cases. An account retaining only those aggregates therefore cannot distinguish them. Whatever consumption it predicts from that account, it must return the same answer twice. Since the actual answers are 9/169/16 apart, it misses by at least half that gap, 9/329/32, in one case. Recording who owns the complement and how that recipient spends recovers the missing distinction.

This is a small version of the question studied in Compression is a promise about questions. Two situations can look identical through one description and differ in a consequence we care about. Here ordinary ownership and consumption accounting supplies the repair.

It does make the buyer question unavoidable for this comparison. More output and more household purchasing power are different claims. Who gets to buy what machines produce? follows the channels through which people might receive the gains: prices, wages, new work, ownership, transfers and public demand. A channel must be described and tested before its existence is treated as compensation for another channel's loss.

When, how and what belong together

A calculation at two values of CC leaves out the transition between them. Who invests before the complement becomes valuable? Who owns it already? Which temporary businesses appear because deployment is incomplete? Can a firm reverse its choice, and can a household wait for the next source of income? Those questions change which future becomes reachable.

There is no single morning on which every task and institution becomes post-AGI. Capability, access, recurring use and institutional adaptation can cross their thresholds at different times. One Yardstick, One Clock asks how comparable execution and a model of transition could make the time available to adapt measurable. That clock remains an instrument to develop and test. The inquiry here develops alongside it: where do constraints and income move, and which description keeps explaining the change?

The history of media makes the interaction easier to see. Radio became Spotify follows a need that persists while distribution, habits, measurements and businesses change around it. A catalogue still needs an audience asks which scarce resource earns income after copying becomes cheap. These histories supply mechanisms to investigate. They do not settle an AGI date or prove that the same ownership and demand arrangements will recur.

What would make the example useful outside the page?

The next empirical step needs a named production setting, meaningful measures of cognition and its complements, evidence for substitution, a payment rule and observations of who receives and spends the income. Alternative explanations need the same opportunity to fit. If a conventional model answers the question, that is useful progress. If it fails, the failure must say which consequence it lost and what additional information restores it.

items.title: A forecast meets its outcome
items.content_html:
A forecast meets its outcome

At the end of June, a model assigns probability 0.8 to an event in September: half of a stated group of firms will operate a particular invoice-preparation workflow at the required quality. September arrives. How should that forecast meet what happened?

The example is hypothetical, but it gives the timing problem something to answer to. A probability of 0.8 is neither a guarantee nor a way to remain right regardless of the result. It is a distribution whose confidence has consequences when scored. A useful One Yardstick clock would earn trust through such encounters: an event defined before its outcome, information available at the time, and a comparison with what a simpler forecast could say.

The prediction carries a date

The population, workflow and acceptance condition are part of the event; September and the June information cutoff are part of the prediction. Another forecast made in August can use August information. It answers the same target event from a different starting position and shorter horizon. An August model cannot be credited with a June prediction by fitting to the completed quarter afterwards. Similarly, a revised historical series may support a better present model while remaining unavailable to the original forecaster at the time. This is why a forecast needs an information vintage as well as a model version. When a forecast is issued, it can use only what could then be known. A later outcome can correct the observation; it cannot silently improve the earlier information set.

A forecast record separates what was known from what was later observed:

Record Origin and information cutoff Target Probability or outcome
First forecast End of June Stated September event 0.8
Updated forecast End of August The same September event Its newly issued probability
Outcome End of September The original workflow, population and acceptance condition Observed yes or no, or an explicitly missing observation

The August update gets to learn from August. It does not replace the June record. A missing September observation is also different from a non-occurrence.

A probability is more than a yes or a no

An event assigned probability 0.8 can fail to happen without logically contradicting the forecast. The remaining 0.2 is part of what was predicted. Yet a forecaster assigning 0.8 to everything should not be able to claim perpetual success by invoking that possibility after every failure.

Scoring makes the whole probability consequential. For a binary event with outcome y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}, the Brier loss is:

LBrier(p,y)=(p−y)2. L_{\mathrm{Brier}}(p,y)=(p-y)^2.

Lower is better. If the event happens, p = 0.8 receives loss 0.04 and p = 0.5 receives 0.25. If it does not happen, the losses are 0.64 and 0.25. Confidence creates both the possibility of a better score and a larger penalty for being wrong.

The logarithmic loss makes another trade-off:

Llog⁡(p,y)=−ylog⁡p−(1−y)log⁡(1−p). L_{\log}(p,y)=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p).

For an observed event use −log⁡p-\log p; for a non-event use −log⁡(1−p)-\log(1-p). A certain prediction has zero loss if it is right and infinite loss if it is wrong. Assigning zero probability to an outcome that occurs is therefore penalised without bound. Gneiting and Raftery's treatment of proper scoring rules explains why a forecaster minimises its expected loss by reporting its assessed distribution honestly.

Calibration needs resolution

In a constructed ten-case example, forecasts consist of five assigned probability 0.8 and five assigned 0.2. Four events occur in the first group and one in the second. The observed frequencies equal the predicted probabilities in these small groups, and the mean Brier loss is 0.16. A constant 0.5 forecast on these same outcomes receives 0.25. The constant forecast gets the overall frequency right: five of ten events occurred. But it makes no distinction between cases. The varying probabilities preserve useful resolution while matching the group frequencies.

To judge calibration beyond this example, we need enough relevant cases and an account of their uncertainty and dependence. Ten forecasts about the same sector and overlapping quarter are not ten independent replications. A system can also score well overall while overestimating one group's prospects or failing on a changed operating condition. Which cases go wrong matters when someone uses the forecast.

The alternative can be very simple

A sophisticated timing model has to add information beyond a simpler comparator. For an adoption event, a baseline might use the previous observed rate or a predeclared trend. For a crossing time, it might use a fixed hazard under stated conditions. The baseline should be credible for the question, not intentionally bad. Both forecasts need the same event, origins, horizons and observations. One model predicting three months ahead cannot be compared casually with another updated the day before the outcome. Trying many model variants on a small evaluation window can also select a lucky winner. A rolling-origin comparison, in which each origin uses only prior information, makes the prospective test more faithful, though overlapping outcomes and structural change still affect its interpretation.

A forecast of the waiting time also has to account for incomplete observation. A forecast meets its outcome
At the end of June, a model assigns probability 0.8 to an event in September: half of a stated group of firms will operate a particular invoice-preparation workflow at the required quality. September arrives. How should that forecast meet what happened?
The example is hypothetical, but it gives the timing problem something to answer to. A probability of 0.8 is neither a guarantee nor a way to remain right regardless of the result. It is a distribution whose confidence has consequences when scored. A useful One Yardstick clock would earn trust through such encounters: an event defined before its outcome, information available at the time, and a comparison with what a simpler forecast could say.
The prediction carries a date
The population, workflow and acceptance condition are part of the event; September and the June information cutoff are part of the prediction. Another forecast made in August can use August information. It answers the same target event from a different starting position and shorter horizon. An August model cannot be credited with a June prediction by fitting to the completed quarter afterwards. Similarly, a revised historical series may support a better present model while remaining unavailable to the original forecaster at the time. This is why a forecast needs an information vintage as well as a model version. When a forecast is issued, it can use only what could then be known. A later outcome can correct the observation; it cannot silently improve the earlier information set.

Updated forecast	End of August	The same September event	Its newly issued probability	
Outcome	End of September	The original workflow, population and acceptance condition	Observed yes or no, or an explicitly missing observation	
The August update gets to learn from August. It does not replace the June record. A missing September observation is also different from a non-occurrence.
A probability is more than a yes or a no
An event assigned probability 0.8 can fail to happen without logically contradicting the forecast. The remaining 0.2 is part of what was predicted. Yet a forecaster assigning 0.8 to everything should not be able to claim perpetual success by invoking that possibility after every failure.
Scoring makes the whole probability consequential. For a binary event with outcome y\in\{0,1\}, the Brier loss is:

L_{\mathrm{Brier}}(p,y)=(p-y)^2.

The logarithmic loss makes another trade-off:

L_{\log}(p,y)=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p).

items.title: Counting the spread of AI
items.content_html:
Counting the spread of AI

Imagine that an adoption survey broadens "AI used in production" to "AI used in any business function". A firm drafting an internal email now qualifies. Its reported category can change while its production process stays exactly as it was.

The broader question reveals uses that were previously invisible and changes what can be compared over time. An increase can come from firms changing how they work, the survey counting more kinds of work, or both. Which event the survey counts, whom it asks and when it asks them all shape the answer.

The question defines the counted event

The US Census Bureau made this change in its Business Trends and Outlook Survey in November 2025, broadening the question from AI used in producing goods or services to AI used in any business function. Its May 2026 account also distinguishes recent use from expected future use.1 The wording change creates a break in what the historical series counts. Comparing the periods requires a common definition where one can be recovered, and a visible break where it cannot. A better current observation can therefore make a simple historical comparison less reliable.

A firm is not a unit of work

Suppose, hypothetically, ten small firms each use one assistant occasionally and one large firm delegates a substantial recurring workflow. A firm-count adoption rate treats each adopter as one. A worker-weighted rate, a task-time rate and a value-added rate can tell different stories. None is inherently the correct rate for every question. Firm counts describe diffusion across firms. Worker weights describe reach across people. A task denominator can describe coverage of work, but requires a definition of tasks and a treatment of assistance versus autonomy. Value weights ask a different question again. A number cannot become the automation share in a production model merely because it is the only frequent series available.

Consider a small constructed survey, separate from the Census observations. All ten responding firms remain unchanged between two questionnaires:

Firm category Firms Qualify as using AI in production Qualify as using AI in any function
Recurring production use 2 2 2
Internal email assistance only 3 0 3
No use 5 0 0
Total 10 2 5

The measured rate rises from 20 to 50 percent solely because the event changes. A bridge questionnaire asking both questions could locate the additional uses. It would not justify multiplying all earlier production-use rates by 2.5: the overlap can change across populations and dates.

Expectations, access and use are different observations

An executive's plan to adopt is not observed adoption. Access to a tool does not show that people use it. Recent use does not show that it completes work at the required quality. Self-reported time saved does not show where the saving went. Yotzov and coauthors' 2026 executive survey separately asks about current use, reported past effects and expected future effects.2 Those categories can disagree without any respondent being inconsistent: firms may expect a larger change than they have experienced. An adoption model that blends them into one state loses that information. It may also confuse anticipation with the effect of deployed technology.

Selection can look like a treatment effect

Firms that adopt may already have better data, more skilled workers or stronger demand. Workers using a tool may be those most able to benefit from it. The difference between users and non-users then includes more than the tool. A survey can describe that selection. It cannot automatically remove it. A causal comparison needs a design whose assumptions address why adoption occurred, alongside a clear definition of the treatment and outcome.

The same caution applies to task exposure. An occupation-level score crosswalked to an industry is several steps away from observed autonomous work in a particular firm. It may be informative, but its grain and intended use should remain visible.

Keeping a series comparable as use changes

A consistent series can follow a local frontier: a defined kind of use among a stated population over time. A survey showing widespread assistance answers a useful question while leaving the coverage of autonomous execution open. Preserving both conclusions makes the evidence available to the worker-outcome inquiry without turning use into an employment effect. A local clock likewise needs a frontier observed consistently enough to time. Definitions and denominators determine which movement the series can describe. They are part of the economic account, not footnotes beneath its headline number.

  1. The Business Trends and Outlook Survey covers US employer businesses, excluding farms. It asks about AI use during the preceding two weeks and expected use over the next six months. The Census Bureau's May 2026 account examines responses collected from 14 December 2025 to 3 May 2026, after the wording changed on 17 November 2025. Its use rates count businesses, not the share of their work performed by AI. ↩

  2. The March 2026 revision of Firm Data on AI draws on nearly 6,000 senior executives reporting about their firms in the US, UK, Germany and Australia between November 2025 and January 2026. It asks which AI technologies the firm uses or intends to use, and separately asks about effects on employment and sales volume per employee over the previous three years and expected effects over the next three. Those effects are executives' reports and expectations. ↩
