items.title: The economy inside the measure
items.content_html:
The economy inside the measure

A service answers twice as many questions at half the price. Its customers spend the same total amount. Has the economy gained a larger service, merely produced more text, or moved effort into correcting the answers?

In this hypothetical comparison, expenditure counts payments, answer counts track output, and useful service asks whether the answer helped the person who requested it. As AI changes production, an increase in one measure can come from a change in the work or from a change in which parts of the work are counted.

Producing AI and producing with it

A supplier builds software, a factory uses it and a customer buys the factory's output. The software is an input to the factory's production. Adding the gross sales at every layer would count some of the same activity more than once. The Bureau of Economic Analysis' January 2025 study distinguishes AI production from its uses within national accounting. It considers a thematic satellite account spanning manufacturing, software, data services and research, with classification and data limitations. Locating the technology in an existing accounting system is substantive work: the categories determine where its contribution appears, rather than making GDP meaningless simply because the technology is new.

Here is a deliberately stripped-down supply chain, with no imports or other intermediate purchases:

Producer Output sold Intermediate purchases Value added
Software supplier 20 0 20
Factory buying that software 100 20 80
Combined 120 in gross sales 20 100

The customer buys the factory's final output for 100. Adding 120 in gross sales would count the software once as the supplier's output and again inside the factory's price. Subtracting intermediate use gives 100 of value added. In this example, both the cost and the supplier's output concern software consumed in the period; a capitalised asset would require a different accounting treatment. The example explains the boundary, not a proposed AI satellite account.

Quantity, quality and welfare

Return to the service that produces twice as many answers at half the price. Nominal expenditure can remain unchanged. If the answers are equally useful, more service is available; if many need correction, an answer count overstates useful output. New users gaining access introduce a welfare question extending beyond the expenditure total. Quality adjustment depends on purpose. Accuracy, timeliness, accessibility and consequential errors measure different aspects of a service. A price index cannot settle their social value by quietly assigning them one weight. Likewise, a free output may create value, impose costs, replace a paid service or consume attention. Accounting and welfare require connected arguments with different boundaries.

Operations, jobs and outcomes

Compute utilisation compares performed operations with a capacity benchmark. A completed-job measure follows a workflow; revenue follows transactions; an outcome measure follows the result someone needs. Their relationships depend on the workload and the process between them. A provider could raise utilisation by accepting less valuable work. It could reduce average job cost while making important jobs wait longer. A team could produce more drafts while finishing fewer accepted documents. In each case the convenient number improves while another consequence deteriorates. A useful comparison therefore carries the workload mix, denominator, target and relevant constraints with it. Where quality changes, the comparison needs to show that change rather than silently treating every unit as equivalent.

The incentive inside the observation

When funding or permission depends on a metric, participants respond to it. A delivered-capacity measure can encourage completion while neglecting whom the service reaches. A count of drafts can encourage drafting at the expense of review. Sometimes that response is the intended incentive; sometimes it moves work away from the purpose the measure was selected to serve. Additional measures can make a trade-off visible, but they also cost effort to collect. Combining them into a single index introduces a choice about their relative importance. The observation rule is consequently part of the institutional arrangement, not a neutral window onto it.

A repair might change the denominator, preserve a separate quality boundary, follow a linked outcome or decline to aggregate. Broadening the event counted as AI adoption can raise a reported rate without changing a single firm's activity. Repairing that comparison requires a common counted event or a visible break in the series. A changed production relation poses a different problem: the process itself has changed, not just the way it was counted.

The measure remains useful when its interpretation can travel with the number: what activity it counts, for which question, under which definition. That is how an account can evolve with the work without losing the consequence it was meant to reveal.

items.title: After the planning bottleneck
items.content_html:
After the planning bottleneck

A workshop has five usable plans and machine time for ten jobs. Better planning gives it twenty plans, but the machines still carry only ten. The workshop has gained a real capability, and its next useful investment has changed.

This deliberately hypothetical picture is a way into the economics of cheaper cognition. Plans, designs and coordination can become easier to supply while equipment, energy, access or human presence still bounds the result. Following the constraint lets us ask what expands, who can supply the next missing input and which account of production continues to describe the activity.

A workshop limited by planning and by machine time

Planning capacity aa Machine capacity mm Completed-job capacity yy Extra output from one more plan
5 10 5 1
10 10 10 0
20 10 10 0

At the corner a=ma=m, adding only a plan leaves output unchanged; adding one unit of both inputs permits another job. This is why a single smooth marginal-product story needs care at the crossing.

After planning reaches twenty, raising machine capacity from ten to eleven adds one possible job. The production value of that increment depends on the job's value and on whether anyone wants it. The relation locates a feasible improvement; it does not fix a supplier's price or establish a profitable investment.

Substitution and complementary demand

Where tasks are substitutes, an organisation may replace expensive work with cheaper work. Where they are complements, it may demand more of the remaining input. A hospital's scheduling, a factory's maintenance and a purely digital service need not share the same production relation. Even a highly digital activity can have a scarce complement: permission to use relevant data, a distribution channel, an accountable signatory, a customer relationship or the capacity to verify unusual cases. These are not all physical constraints. They may be contractual or institutional, and some can change when organisations redesign their work.

Acemoglu's task-based macroeconomic analysis makes the coverage of affected tasks and the size of their cost savings central to aggregate productivity. A dramatic saving on a narrow slice does not automatically become a dramatic saving for the whole economy.

The constraint can move more than once

Increasing machine capacity may reveal a shortage of operators. Training operators may reveal weak demand. Growing demand may reveal scarce working capital. A static ranking of “the AI bottlenecks” misses this sequence. That also explains why a temporary complement need not be a durable winner. A firm can command a high price while supply is scarce and lose that margin after entry. Integration work can be essential during a transition and become routine later. A component's present importance does not establish its long-run bargaining position. The horizon changes the available alternatives. What binds during a pilot may differ from what binds at scale, after investment, entry or a redesigned process makes another input available. A scenario needs those adjustment times alongside its present capacities.

Scarcity, rent and return are three questions

A scarce resource has a marginal value within a production problem. Its owner captures a rent only if contracts, competition and access allow that value to become income. An investor earns a return only after the price paid and the available claim on that income are considered. An essential network might be competitively priced or regulated. A supplier might spend its additional revenue expanding capacity. A customer may own the complementary asset and retain most of the saving. Saying “this input is necessary” resolves none of those cases.

The workshop's limiting input moves within the same production relation. items.title: Who captures value when the bottleneck moves?
items.content_html:
Who captures value when the bottleneck moves?

When one input becomes cheap, the remaining scarce inputs acquire more importance in production. Turning that importance into income requires control over access, a way to charge and a surplus after supply costs. A production constraint, a rent-bearing asset and a financial claim therefore describe different parts of the path from useful input to economic return.

The necessary input may have little pricing power

Imagine a digital service that needs a specialised data connection. Without it, the service cannot operate. If several suppliers offer equivalent connections and customers can switch easily, necessity need not produce large margins. Now change the arrangement: one supplier has an exclusive right to the relevant data, and switching requires a long migration. The technical role is similar, but control and outside options differ. The rent story comes from those rights and alternatives, not simply from the word “data”. A physical input can show the same distinction. Installed capacity may be scarce while providers compete for customers. An essential service may have a regulated price. A supplier may face costs or liabilities that absorb the additional revenue.

A small cash-flow comparison makes the difference tangible. In both arrangements, the connection supports the same service. The service brings in 100, and its other operating costs are 60:

Arrangement Connection payment Connection supplier's cost Connection supplier's residual Service operator's residual
Interchangeable suppliers 10 8 2 30
Exclusive access contract 30 8 22 10

The amounts illustrate two stipulated contracts, not estimates or an explanation of how market prices settle. Total residual across the supplier and the operator remains 32. The contractual price moves twenty of it from the service operator to the connection supplier.

A larger residual is not automatically economic rent. Some of it may compensate capital, risk or an omitted cost. Likewise, an exclusive contract does not justify any arbitrary price: customers can reduce demand, reorganise the service or find another way to meet their need. Those alternatives decide whether the arrangement survives.

An outside option can bound the price without selecting it. Keep the same service revenue of 100 and other costs of 60, and suppose the operator can earn a residual of 10 through an alternative arrangement. For this connection to be at least as attractive, its residual 100−60−p100-60-p must be at least 10, so its maximum acceptable connection payment is 30. With supplier cost 8 and no other costs or risks, a payment below 8 cannot cover supply. The possible bargain lies between 8 and 30. The two contracts in the table occupy different points in that interval.

Nothing in that interval explains which price is agreed. Competing equivalent suppliers, the buyer's credible ability to switch, negotiation and the terms fixing future prices add the price-formation mechanism. A better outside option can lower the ceiling; an unreliable substitute may leave it high. The bottleneck supplies an opportunity to bargain, while the alternatives and contract determine how its surplus is divided.

Follow the right, not merely the asset

Owning a piece of equipment, operating it, holding a contract for its output and owning a company that supplies it confer different claims. A contract can reserve capacity without granting a right to all future scarcity income. A provider can control an interface while licensing the underlying asset from someone else. These distinctions matter when a capability improvement changes demand. Who can raise the price? Who bears expansion cost? Who can substitute? Who has promised a fixed service level? Which party receives the saving? The same technical bottleneck can support different incidence under different contracts. Describing an industry's “winners” without those relationships risks attaching the benefit to the most visible name rather than its recipient.

New supply can remove a transitional rent

A shortage can invite entry, expansion or substitution. Higher prices may finance the capacity that later weakens those prices. A supplier that succeeds in removing a constraint can help its customers while diminishing its own scarcity advantage. There are also persistent constraints. Some locations, rights or coordination arrangements may be difficult to reproduce. Persistence still needs an explanation: high fixed costs, a legal limit, learning, network effects, customer switching costs or another mechanism. The horizon therefore belongs inside the claim. A useful bridge during a transition may not remain a toll road afterward.

Cheap capability can coexist with concentrated dependence

A user may have access to inexpensive outputs while depending on a small set of providers. Low marginal cost and a competitive retail price do not establish a resilient supply arrangement. The Financial Stability Board's 2024 AI assessment identifies third-party dependence, provider concentration and correlated behaviour among financial-sector vulnerabilities. It does not prove that every AI market concentrates. It gives a concrete reason to examine shared infrastructure and failure channels separately from price. Open weights, portability or more providers could weaken a rent. Conversely, proprietary workflows or scarce access could preserve it even as a model's price falls. Both are countercases a serious claim has to face.

The duration of a rent

A rent weakens as substitution becomes feasible, competition dissipates the surplus, customers retain more of the saving or additional capacity outruns demand. Its contractual basis matters just as much: the party operating a necessary input may lack the claim through which the surplus is paid. The production constraint helps explain why an input matters; information markets show how selection and attention can create a different scarcity from installed equipment. The durable-income question follows control, alternatives and time together. A moving bottleneck creates an opportunity to supply something useful. Whether that opportunity becomes a lasting return depends on the relationships around the supply, not just its place in the technical system.

items.title: Compare complete execution
items.content_html:
Compare complete execution

You want to know whether an agent can prepare invoices for review more economically than a person. Count the whole job: the result, the mistakes, the review and the cost. One Yardstick develops that comparison between people and agents. Both need a task they can attempt under the same conditions. A measurable objective, a reliable evaluator and access to the right tools make a comparison possible; they do not tell you who will perform better.

The same task can call for different actions

Consider invoice preparation. The executor checks an invoice against its order and receipt, then prepares a payment proposal or sends a discrepancy for review. Give both executors the same records and access, and judge them against the same requirements.

Important

The task ends at review. Releasing funds is outside this comparison.

When the records agree

The invoice requests payment for twelve units. The order and receipt also record twelve. Prepare a proposal with those records for the person who can approve it.

When a discrepancy remains unresolved

The invoice and order record twelve units, but the receipt records ten. Flag the two-unit difference and include the records needed to investigate it. A faster payment proposal would not resolve the discrepancy.

One evaluation, applied to both

Agree on four parts of the comparison before the trial:

  • Quality: did the records warrant each proposal or escalation?
  • Errors: what did a wrong action or missed exception cost?
  • Human effort: how much review, correction and escalation remained?
  • Total cost: what did execution, supporting systems and human effort require?

A correct escalation is useful work. A quick proposal can still be wrong. The evaluator must remain reliable on the cases the executor will actually encounter, including difficult exceptions. What makes work executable? explains that distinction.

Count the work needed to reach an accepted result

Suppose each executor handles the same 100 invoices. After review and correction, each batch has 100 acceptable proposals or escalations. No funds have been released. These invented figures illustrate the calculation:

Work or cost for the batch Human execution Agent execution
Human effort performing the initial task 240 minutes 0 minutes
Human review 50 minutes 100 minutes
Human correction 10 minutes 20 minutes
Model and tool charges USD 10 USD 20
Accepted results after review and correction 100 100

At USD 30 per hour of human effort, the human arrangement costs USD 160: five hours plus USD 10 in tool charges. The agent arrangement costs USD 80: two hours plus USD 20 in model and tool charges. That is USD 1.60 and USD 0.80 per accepted result. The zero in the first row means no human performed the agent's initial step; its machine cost is included in the charges.

The cheaper arrangement still required twice as much review and correction. Keep each initial result beside its reviewed outcome so that the final count does not hide missed discrepancies, unnecessary escalations or correct requests for help. A serious error that breaches a requirement remains a failure even when average cost is low.

Note

The example's cost assumptions. This example assumes no additional setup or operating expense. A real comparison needs those costs, the intended mix of invoices and an agreed review procedure. Different cases, prices or review effort can reverse the result; the arithmetic is not evidence of either executor's performance.

Adoption is a different event

A successful trial does not show that organisations will use an executor repeatedly. To study adoption, define the population and what counts as recurring use at an acceptable quality and cost. Then observe that event.

One Yardstick proposes a transition clock for the economy. Testing that ambition also requires examining particular frontiers: a capability becoming accessible, a deployment becoming reliable or an organisation changing its work. These processes need not move at the same pace. A forecast needs an observable process and an outcome defined before it is known.

The buyers remain in the picture

Cheaper execution does not settle who can buy the output. An agent does not need the income with which a displaced worker bought a service. Follow the production gain into prices, wages, ownership and public arrangements to understand how it changes a household's available resources.

The broader Post-AGI Economics inquiry studies those frontiers, moving constraints and income arrangements alongside the clock. Comparing one task contributes evidence about execution. Linking it to an economic transition requires an account of adoption, the work around the tool and where the income goes.

What makes work executable?

When a job has a measurable objective, a reliable way to judge the result and tools that can act, what still requires its executor to be human? The Agent Execution Hypothesis proposes that an artificial agent can, in principle, match or exceed human execution under the same inputs, tools and constraints. It is a claim to test, not a result obtained merely by specifying the task.

The economic stakes follow from that claim. If an agent can deliver the required quality at a lower complete cost, a firm has a reason to substitute it for some human work. If checking, integration or handling exceptions consumes the saving, cheaper model output need not make the job cheaper. And if substitution removes a worker’s income, the agent does not become the customer that worker was. Execution, its complementary work and the buyer belong in the same inquiry.

A signal does not choose its recipient

Choosing what to optimise is different from executing well against that objective. Hayek’s account of prices explains how people can coordinate using knowledge dispersed among them, without each knowing every circumstance behind a price.1 The extension in One Yardstick, One Clock is that a person or a machine could respond to a useful signal if it can interpret it and has the means to act. The signal’s usefulness does not by itself establish either executor’s competence.

An evaluator makes that proposal concrete for a task. It must distinguish the outcome we value from a convenient proxy. Tacit skill does not disappear because we cannot easily score it: if its contribution cannot be captured well enough for the comparison, the execution claim has not yet been made testable there.

Follow the objective into an invoice

Pay the right supplier, the right amount, at the right time, without duplicates. The objective fits in one sentence. Following it into an invoice workflow reveals a much larger task: an ambiguous supplier, a changed bank instruction, conflicting documents and an approval still needed before money moves.

Give both executors the same process to carry through, including the moments when they need help. The evaluator can then judge what they did and what they handed over for review.

Important

The comparison ends before money moves. The task is to prepare a payment proposal or collect the records needed to review an unresolved discrepancy.

Part of the comparison Illustrative specification
Cases Routine invoices, duplicate submissions, disputed quantities and changed bank instructions; report each category separately
Information The same invoice, purchase order, receipt and dated supplier record for both executors
Allowed actions Read those records, prepare a proposal, or escalate an unresolved discrepancy
Acceptance Supplier, amount and supporting records agree; every unresolved instruction change is escalated
Consequential error A proposal treated as ready despite an unresolved bank instruction, duplicate or unsupported amount
Whole cost Preparation and review time, tool use, retries and the work required to resolve escalations

A record saying “supplier instruction changed” can justify asking for confirmation without identifying which instruction is genuine. Correct escalation is then a useful result. A resolved test case and an unresolved live case must not be scored as if they supplied the same information.

The objective meets the documents

In this hypothetical workflow, a test can supply answers that the real process has to discover. If an evaluator learns which bank instruction was valid only after a payment, its feedback can classify the loss but cannot prevent it. Delayed consequences, partial information and a shifting case mix therefore belong inside the test. A system that handles ordinary invoices well may still need a different procedure for a rare, consequential exception. Abstention and escalation can be part of competent execution. The comparison should account for the time and work they require, rather than score every request for help as a failure or treat that help as free.

The same task under the same conditions

Access changes what an executor can do. A human able to call a colleague has a different means of resolving an ambiguity from an agent limited to the supplied documents. An agent with additional records may perform better without having demonstrated superiority under identical inputs. A fair comparison specifies the task distribution, information, tools, time budget and permitted escalation. It also specifies which errors matter. Average accuracy can obscure a rare mistake whose loss dominates the value of many correctly handled cases.

The configuration is part of the comparison. Recommending a payment, preparing it and releasing it involve different effects and responsibilities. An assistant can create value by improving preparation while a person retains approval. Autonomous execution requires its own performance and authority conditions.

From a cheap draft to completed work

The full cost includes checking, retries, monitoring, integration, incident handling, human escalation and delay. Some costs are fixed and spread over more cases; others grow with complexity or consequence. The baseline is the existing process with its actual overhead and errors, not an imaginary flawless human. If preparation becomes faster but review takes longer, the net saving may be small. If routine work becomes easier and people can handle exceptions better, the gain may come through a changed allocation of work rather than replacement. What matters is accepted work at the required quality and risk. Compare complete execution works through the preparation, review and correction costs for a hundred invoices.

Authorisation determines which of those effects an actor may attempt. It is separate from measured performance. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework addresses risk across development and use, making it a useful reference for this deployment boundary rather than a certification of any particular executor.

An execution claim with something to compare

A local claim can say that, for this workflow and case distribution, a configuration reaches the required outcome at a stated cost and risk. Matched performance and deployment evidence can then support or contradict it. A universal claim about all instrumentable workflows would need substantially more: a successful example cannot establish every case, and an imagined better-trained executor cannot indefinitely stand in for a specified one.

The yardstick earns its place by showing where capability works, where assistance is preferable and where the process still needs another means of acting. The organisation around the tool then determines how that local performance becomes productive use.

Follow the saving one step further. Does it lower the customer’s price, increase someone’s income or accrue to the owner of a scarce complement? A person doing less invoice work might take on other work, share in the gain or lose income. Those are different paths to household purchasing power. The invoice comparison can test execution and its cost. Understanding the economy it changes requires following both the work that remains and the income that reaches its buyers.

items.title: Same technology, different economy
items.content_html:
Same technology, different economy

Two economies can have the same technical capacity and distribute its benefits differently. If we want to understand welfare or buyer capacity, ownership and institutions belong inside the argument, not in a paragraph added after a production forecast. Economists call part of this specification a closure: the rules that say what adjusts, what is held fixed, how markets clear and who receives residual income. A closure is necessary to solve a model. It is not necessarily a description of the only possible world.

One production gain, several arrangements

Take a hypothetical service that costs 100 to produce before a new tool and 70 afterward, for unchanged quality and quantity. The saving of 30 gives us a common production change against which to compare different arrangements. Under competitive pass-through, the service's price could fall. Under a protected contract, the supplier could retain much of the saving. Under worker ownership, a residual might reach the workers through their ownership claim rather than their hourly wage. Under public provision, a budget saving might support other services.

A supplier may use the saving to expand, improve quality, service debt or compensate risk. A public budget saving is not automatically paid to households. A lower price helps consumers in proportion to their use, not necessarily in proportion to need. The same cost reduction therefore cannot identify the recipient without describing the surrounding arrangement.

Keep the immediate claim separate from what its recipient later chooses to do:

Arrangement First claim on the benefit Next decision affecting the economy
Competitive pass-through Customers through lower prices Buy more of this service, spend elsewhere or save
Supplier retains the difference Supplier's residual account Invest, distribute, repay an obligation or retain cash
Worker-held residual Workers in their capacity as owners Allocate between distribution and the enterprise's needs
Public provision The relevant public budget Change the service, taxation or another expenditure through its budget process

The rows do not promise any behavioural response. Nor are they mutually exclusive labels for whole economies: a supplier can have worker owners and face strong competition. The comparison specifies a channel and then asks how it operates.

Distribution changes the next production decision

The first-round allocation can affect demand, investment and bargaining. A worker receiving more income may consume differently from an asset owner receiving the same amount. A firm retaining the saving may expand capacity, hold cash or return it to owners. Their choices depend on expectations and constraints, not only accounting. That feedback makes a static allocation incomplete for some purposes. If the question is immediate incidence, a short-run comparison may suffice. If it is the path of demand and capacity, behaviour and adjustment over time matter. A model that originally held ownership and demand fixed can still answer its narrow question. It becomes inadequate when we ask it to compare institutions it never represented. Comparing those institutions requires a change in the model's question or closure.

Governance chooses more than a score

Maximising output, protecting a consumption standard, reducing inequality, preserving meaningful participation and limiting environmental harm are different objectives. A productivity evaluator cannot decide how to trade them off. It can sometimes show the consequences of a chosen rule. It cannot make the rule legitimate simply because it can compute an optimum. A constrained optimisation also inherits the omissions of its objective and constraints. Unmeasured harms do not become acceptable by disappearing from the data. The separation between deciding and executing is thus substantive. Who may change the objective, who may act, who bears losses and who can challenge the decision are institutional questions.

Different arrangements, different paths

A highly automated economy can support strong household demand or concentrate gains while buyers lose income. Public demand, exports, shared ownership, new goods, price adjustment and non-market provision introduce further possibilities. Those channels make buyer capacity a question about the economy's arrangements, not a binary destination selected by its technical capacity. A useful comparison states the resource constraint, funding mechanism, incidence, behavioural response and feasibility of each alternative. It also tests whether the effect survives a simpler explanation such as ordinary competition or a temporary investment cycle.

The household consequences depend on these ownership and adjustment conditions, and on the price arrangement that Where does the saving go? follows. The technology expands a feasible set. Institutions determine who can act within it, receive its gains and challenge its costs.

items.title: The changing work behind an occupation
items.content_html:
The changing work behind an occupation

Two accounting teams do similar work. One has clean records, stable interfaces and a manager able to redesign approvals. The other spends its days reconciling inconsistent documents and finding missing authorisations. An occupation-level exposure score can place them together while the technology reaches their work very differently.

The occupational label hides the work of those two hypothetical teams. Capability reaches tasks through an organisation; changed tasks can alter output, hours, hiring and pay. The evidence becomes much more interesting when we keep those objects in view. An exposure score, a resolved support issue and an entry-level hire each reveal a different part of the movement.

A task description is not a deployment record

Exposure measures compare descriptions of work with an assessment of what a technology could do. That can locate an opportunity or a vulnerability. It does not observe a firm's permissions, data quality, integration costs or willingness to change its process. The two teams' different capacity to reorganise makes this gap substantive, rather than merely a delay before an identical deployment reaches both.

Actual adoption also means several things. A person drafting emails, a team using suggestions in every case, and a system closing cases without human intervention are not interchangeable treatments. Pulito and coauthors' Danish study links surveys to employer-worker records and finds adoption associated with firm capacity, digital infrastructure and workforce composition; exposure measures differ in how well they predict it. That is evidence about who adopts, not an estimate of what adoption does to wages.

Productivity can rise through different routes

A support assistant may help novices recognise a problem more quickly. A planning system may reduce avoidable rework. Automation may remove a task, while new verification work takes its place. Each can raise output per worker through a different mechanism. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond's May 2025 journal article follows 5,172 customer-support agents at one business-software firm. Its staggered introduction of assistance raises issues resolved per hour by about 15%, with unequal gains across experience levels.1 It is useful precisely because the work and treatment are specific. It does not estimate an economy-wide employment response.

Aldasoro and coauthors' January 2026 European firm study instead matches survey and financial data and uses US peer adoption as an instrument. It estimates higher labour productivity, consistent with capital deepening, without short-run employment losses; complementary investment and firm size matter. The causal interpretation depends on that instrument's assumptions. Neither the short horizon nor the sampled firms establishes that displacement cannot happen elsewhere or later.

If demand expands, saved time may support more output. If demand is fixed, the same saving may reduce hours or headcount. If the firm improves quality, a quantity measure can miss part of the gain. A task-level result does not select its destination.

A deployment can also change demand for the work. A buyer finding the answer needed to purchase creates a different possibility from completing an existing support case faster. The labour response still depends on the resulting work, its cost and the firm’s decisions.

Little average change can coexist with changing tasks

Humlum and Vestergaard's 13 March 2026 study links surveys in eleven exposed Danish occupations to administrative records through December 2024. In its adopter comparison, differential earnings and recorded-hours effects are near zero, with effects larger than about 2% ruled out over the two years after ChatGPT's launch. Yet tasks change and new oversight work appears.2 A small average difference between adopters and non-adopters is compatible with substantial reorganisation. A change common to both groups is not identified directly by that comparison.

Expectations are another observation. The March 2026 revision of Yotzov and coauthors' firm survey covers almost 6,000 executives in the US, UK, Germany and Australia. Most report little employment or productivity impact over the preceding three years, while expecting larger changes over the next three. These are reports and forecasts, not a randomised estimate of adoption's effect.3 Its October 2026 revision adds countries and a later survey and is a separate observation.

Early-career harm deserves a specific explanation

Lee Tucker's April 2026 analysis finds a marked decline in early-career hiring in highly exposed industry-state cells after ChatGPT. Its broader comparisons also reveal pandemic-era trend changes. A historical decomposition suggests monetary-policy shocks through 2023 could account for up to one quarter of the relative early-career employment decline through the second quarter of 2025. The analysis finds no evidence that those shocks explain the rapid relative decline in hires. That distinction matters when asking what caused the fall in hiring. Exposure is not observed firm deployment, so the study does not directly trace the whole automation mechanism.

Audoly, Guerin and Topa's May 2026 job-posting analysis finds that exposed occupations' relative weakness predates ChatGPT and no clear additional junior-senior divergence. Postings are not completed hires. The studies differ in outcomes, groupings and comparisons; treating one as settling the other would discard the question each can answer.

A firm might reduce junior hiring before deploying a tool because it expects future substitution. It might also reduce hiring because demand weakened. Separating those explanations requires expectations and deployment observations alongside the same firms' hiring, separations and task changes.

A change in the question can change the adoption rate

The April 2026 Bonney and coauthors study separates firm adoption, business-function deployment and worker-task use in the US Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey. It reports 18% of firms using AI in at least one function during November 2025–January 2026, or 32% when weighted by employment.4 Those are different denominators. Neither is the fraction of all work performed autonomously by AI. Changing survey wording also interrupts a simple comparison with the earlier use series; a jump in the reported number can reflect the instrument as well as the economy.

Highfill and Samuels' July 2026 BEA study adds another gap: stated intentions do not straightforwardly predict realised changes in production. It compares expected with actual adoption and separately connects earlier adoption motives to industry accounts.5 The industry account and a worker's task record can both be useful while answering different questions. Joining them requires a defensible relationship between the populations, periods and measures.

Following the gain to the worker

The support study can reveal a mechanism by which assistance helps a novice. The hiring study can reveal a troubling change without observing that mechanism. Connecting them needs evidence on deployment and the same workers or firms, not just a shared date or the word “AI”.

A convincing account connects actual use to quality-adjusted output, full operating cost, prices, hours, employment and pay. It then asks whether the effects persist, spill over to competitors, or shift expenditure between products rather than expand it. The result may be augmentation in one setting and displacement in another. That heterogeneity is the finding to explain, not noise to average out. Even established production gains leave the household's ability to buy the output to be explained. Lower prices, changed hours, wages and income claims can move its purchasing power in different directions; the worker's place in production is one part of that larger account.

The changing work behind an occupation
Two accounting teams do similar work. One has clean records, stable interfaces and a manager able to redesign approvals. The other spends its days reconciling inconsistent documents and finding missing authorisations. An occupation-level exposure score can place them together while the technology reaches their work very differently.
The occupational label hides the work of those two hypothetical teams. Capability reaches tasks through an organisation; changed tasks can alter output, hours, hiring and pay. The evidence becomes much more interesting when we keep those objects in view. An exposure score, a resolved support issue and an entry-level hire each reveal a different part of the movement.
A task description is not a deployment record
Exposure measures compare descriptions of work with an assessment of what a technology could do. That can locate an opportunity or a vulnerability. It does not observe a firm's permissions, data quality, integration costs or willingness to change its process. The two teams' different capacity to reorganise makes this gap substantive, rather than merely a delay before an identical deployment reaches both.
Actual adoption also means several things. A person drafting emails, a team using suggestions in every case, and a system closing cases without human intervention are not interchangeable treatments. Pulito and coauthors' Danish study links surveys to employer-worker records and finds adoption associated with firm capacity, digital infrastructure and workforce composition; exposure measures differ in how well they predict it. That is evidence about who adopts, not an estimate of what adoption does to wages.
Productivity can rise through different routes
A support assistant may help novices recognise a problem more quickly. A planning system may reduce avoidable rework. Automation may remove a task, while new verification work takes its place. Each can raise output per worker through a different mechanism. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond's May 2025 journal article follows 5,172 customer-support agents at one business-software firm. Its staggered introduction of assistance raises issues resolved per hour by about 15%, with unequal gains across experience levels. It is useful precisely because the work and treatment are specific. It does not estimate an economy-wide employment response.
Aldasoro and coauthors' January 2026 European firm study instead matches survey and financial data and uses US peer adoption as an instrument. It estimates higher labour productivity, consistent with capital deepening, without short-run employment losses; complementary investment and firm size matter. The causal interpretation depends on that instrument's assumptions. Neither the short horizon nor the sampled firms establishes that displacement cannot happen elsewhere or later.
If demand expands, saved time may support more output. If demand is fixed, the same saving may reduce hours or headcount. If the firm improves quality, a quantity measure can miss part of the gain. A task-level result does not select its destination.
A deployment can also change demand for the work. A buyer finding the answer needed to purchase creates a different possibility from completing an existing support case faster. The labour response still depends on the resulting work, its cost and the firm’s decisions.
Little average change can coexist with changing tasks
Humlum and Vestergaard's 13 March 2026 study links surveys in eleven exposed Danish occupations to administrative records through December 2024. In its adopter comparison, differential earnings and recorded-hours effects are near zero, with effects larger than about 2% ruled out over the two years after ChatGPT's launch. Yet tasks change and new oversight work appears. A small average difference between adopters and non-adopters is compatible with substantial reorganisation. A change common to both groups is not identified directly by that comparison.
Expectations are another observation. The March 2026 revision of Yotzov and coauthors' firm survey covers almost 6,000 executives in the US, UK, Germany and Australia. Most report little employment or productivity impact over the preceding three years, while expecting larger changes over the next three. These are reports and forecasts, not a randomised estimate of adoption's effect. Its October 2026 revision adds countries and a later survey and is a separate observation.
Early-career harm deserves a specific explanation
Lee Tucker's April 2026 analysis finds a marked decline in early-career hiring in highly exposed industry-state cells after ChatGPT. Its broader comparisons also reveal pandemic-era trend changes. A historical decomposition suggests monetary-policy shocks through 2023 could account for up to one quarter of the relative early-career employment decline through the second quarter of 2025. The analysis finds no evidence that those shocks explain the rapid relative decline in hires. That distinction matters when asking what caused the fall in hiring. Exposure is not observed firm deployment, so the study does not directly trace the whole automation mechanism.
Audoly, Guerin and Topa's May 2026 job-posting analysis finds that exposed occupations' relative weakness predates ChatGPT and no clear additional junior-senior divergence. Postings are not completed hires. The studies differ in outcomes, groupings and comparisons; treating one as settling the other would discard the question each can answer.
A firm might reduce junior hiring before deploying a tool because it expects future substitution. It might also reduce hiring because demand weakened. Separating those explanations requires expectations and deployment observations alongside the same firms' hiring, separations and task changes.
A change in the question can change the adoption rate
The April 2026 Bonney and coauthors study separates firm adoption, business-function deployment and worker-task use in the US Census Business Trends and Outlook Survey. It reports 18% of firms using AI in at least one function during November 2025–January 2026, or 32% when weighted by employment. Those are different denominators. Neither is the fraction of all work performed autonomously by AI. Changing survey wording also interrupts a simple comparison with the earlier use series; a jump in the reported number can reflect the instrument as well as the economy.
Highfill and Samuels' July 2026 BEA study adds another gap: stated intentions do not straightforwardly predict realised changes in production. It compares expected with actual adoption and separately connects earlier adoption motives to industry accounts. The industry account and a worker's task record can both be useful while answering different questions. Joining them requires a defensible relationship between the populations, periods and measures.
Following the gain to the worker
The support study can reveal a mechanism by which assistance helps a novice. The hiring study can reveal a troubling change without observing that mechanism. Connecting them needs evidence on deployment and the same workers or firms, not just a shared date or the word “AI”.
A convincing account connects actual use to quality-adjusted output, full operating cost, prices, hours, employment and pay. It then asks whether the effects persist, spill over to competitors, or shift expenditure between products rather than expand it. The result may be augmentation in one setting and displacement in another. That heterogeneity is the finding to explain, not noise to average out. Even established production gains leave the household's ability to buy the output to be explained. Lower prices, changed hours, wages and income claims can move its purchasing power in different directions; the worker's place in production is one part of that larger account.

items.title: The work around the tool
items.content_html:
The work around the tool

A team reduces report drafting from two days to two hours. The report still waits a week for reconciliation and approval. The impressive component improvement has barely changed when anybody receives the work.

That hypothetical queue makes the organisation around a tool visible. Better source data, a different handoff or clear responsibility for an exception can make faster drafting useful. Calling all of it "adoption lag" hides the work of changing the process. The return depends on which of those investments other tasks can reuse and how long it takes for the savings to cover their cost.

The process can defeat the component

If the faster draft creates more discrepancies for reviewers, total work may even grow. The saving changes one stage while reconciliation or approval still limits the system. Removing that limit may require better source data, fewer handoffs, a revised approval rule or an accountable owner for exceptions. Managerial attention, training time and trust become inputs to the improvement, alongside the software. Multiplying the drafting saving by the number of workers would miss both those costs and the remaining queue.

Put the illustrative stages on the same clock, using an eight-hour working day:

Stage Earlier process Faster drafting only Drafting plus redesigned handoff
Gather and reconcile inputs 8 hours 8 hours 4 hours
Draft 16 hours 2 hours 2 hours
Wait for review slot 40 hours 40 hours 8 hours
Review and acceptance 4 hours 6 hours 4 hours
Elapsed working time 68 hours 56 hours 18 hours
Active work across these stages 28 hours 16 hours 10 hours

These are designed process times, not observations. The middle column assumes a faster draft requires two extra review hours. The last assumes input quality and the review handoff also improve. It does not credit all fifty saved elapsed hours to the drafting tool. Review-slot capacity and reconciliation have changed too.

Elapsed time follows when a recipient can use the report. Active work follows labour consumed by these stages. A shorter queue can matter greatly to the recipient without saving an equal number of worker-hours. Conversely, released labour may not increase output while demand or another stage remains fixed.

Complementary investment changes what we observe

Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson's Productivity J-Curve examines how general-purpose technologies require complementary intangible investment, including new processes, skills and business models. If some of that investment is poorly measured, the timing of measured productivity can differ from the timing of underlying economic work. A delayed payoff and a failed project can look similar early on. Distinguishing them requires observing the complementary work as well as the resulting process: whether data improves, handoffs change and accepted work becomes faster or less costly. Spending on software and training describes the investment; the changed outcome describes its return.

Readiness also selects who adopts

A capable firm may adopt first because it already has useful data, skilled staff and the ability to redesign a process. Comparing adopters with non-adopters can then mix the effect of the tool with the effect of that pre-existing capacity. The Danish adoption study by Pulito and coauthors finds strong associations with firm capacity and workforce readiness. The result motivates this selection concern; it does not prove that every adopter's productivity gain is caused by those characteristics.

A credible test may use a rollout, a suitable instrument or a comparison with defensible pre-trends. It also has to ask what the treatment contains. A “tool rollout” accompanied by process redesign estimates a package, not necessarily the isolated model.

Scaling can reveal different complements

A small team can resolve exceptions informally. A large deployment may need consistent permissions, monitoring, escalation and incident response. The organisation that works for a pilot may not work for scale. Some complements are reusable: a sound data interface can support several tools. Others are highly specific and can become stranded if the system changes. Treating all integration spending as durable capital misses that difference. The relevant account includes useful work after review, total cost, reliability, learning and the ability to replace a supplier. It also asks whether benefits spread across the organisation or concentrate in teams that already had the best conditions.

Complements and their payoff

The complement hypothesis becomes specific when improved data or coordination changes the measured result under a credible comparison. It weakens when checking consumes the saving, redesigned processes yield no material gain, or demand does not value the additional output. The production relation locates the limiting input, while changes in workers' hours, employment and pay reveal how the resulting reorganisation reaches them. The same process improvement can support more output or fewer hours, depending on demand and how the work is arranged.

The organisation is doing more than installing a component. It is deciding how the component fits into work, what other work becomes necessary and whether the combined process earns its cost. That is where a local capability becomes an economic change.

items.title: Who gets to buy what machines produce?
items.content_html:
Who gets to buy what machines produce?

If machines do more of the work, people still need a way to buy what they produce. That is the buyer question behind Post-AGI Economics. Lower prices can help, and so can new work, ownership income or transfers. But they reach different people, under different conditions. A production gain can become a cheaper purchase, greater earnings or a return someone else receives. Follow it into the household's budget to find out which.

Lower prices can help without offsetting every lost income

Consider a hypothetical household that receives 100 units of income, spends 60 on housing and other commitments, and has 40 left for a basket of services. If that basket becomes 20 percent cheaper, the original basket costs 32. The household gains room in its budget. Now suppose its income falls to 80 while those commitments stay at 60. It has only 20 available. The price reduction does not restore the basket. The average productivity gain leaves out the position of someone who loses income while a large part of their expenses does not fall.

Household budget Before Cheaper services Cheaper services and lower income
Income 100 100 80
Fixed commitments 60 60 60
Available for the service basket 40 40 20
Cost of the original basket 40 32 32
Balance after buying that basket 0 8 −12

For this fixed basket and fixed commitments, an income loss of eight would just exhaust the price saving. A loss of twenty exceeds it. In symbols, with income YY, commitments FF and basket cost BB:

room after purchase=Y−F−B. \text{room after purchase}=Y-F-B.

The illustration does not say prices or obligations remain fixed in an actual transition. It makes those assumptions visible. Another household may own an asset whose income rises or receive a transfer; the identical service-price reduction then meets a different budget.

The distribution can disappear even when an aggregate account balances. Extend the example to two identical households, each initially earning 100 with commitments of 60 and a basket costing 40. After the change, let the first earn 80 and the second 120, with both baskets now costing 32. Total income remains 200; buying both baskets now costs 64 rather than 80. The aggregate has 16 units to spare after commitments and those purchases. Yet the first household is short by 12 while the second has 28 left. That surplus does not reach the first household merely because it exists in the total. A transfer, shared ownership or another income channel would be an additional arrangement, with its own conditions.

Labour income is one channel, not the whole budget

A technology can affect hours, wages, employment, entry into occupations and the timing of payments. Household resources may also include profits, dividends, rent, transfers or earnings from other members. Saving and credit can smooth some shocks, but smoothing is different from replacing a lasting income stream. The household is therefore not interchangeable with a worker. A worker-level wage observation omits other members and assets. Aggregate labour income omits its distribution. A growing output total omits both.

Nor is consumer demand the only source of demand. Investment, public spending and exports can support production. New goods may create demand that a fixed product basket misses. These are possible offsets that an argument about weak buyers must examine, not assume away.

An income floor has a level and a denominator

Suppose households consume 80 while total output is 100. If household consumption stays at 80 and output rises to 120, consumption's share falls from 80 percent to about 67 percent. That falling share alone does not establish that households became poorer. The reverse trap is to protect a share without specifying the level, prices or distribution. An unchanged aggregate share can coexist with losses concentrated among particular households.

An income floor must therefore say what it protects: nominal resources, a purchasing-power standard, essential consumption, or a share of income or output. These are different objectives. It must also say how it is funded and how prices, taxes, output and recipients respond. A formula that drops capital income or treats output as fixed has chosen its assumptions, not solved every possible economy. The buyer-rich and buyer-thin outcomes in One Yardstick, One Clock describe different distributional possibilities under those conditions. Comparing them requires a stated consumption standard, income channels and price response, rather than treating a change in output share as a conclusion about household welfare.

Demand can amplify a shock, but the chain needs evidence

If households facing an income loss reduce spending, local firms may lose revenue and hire less. Debt obligations or costly housing can make adjustment harder. But the size and duration depend on which households lose income, what they stop buying, which prices adjust and what other demand replaces theirs. A small saving on digital services may matter little next to housing. A production gain in an exporting firm may reach domestic households through wages or taxes rather than local sales. A capital-intensive provider may reinvest gains for years before distributing them. The relevant time horizon is part of each mechanism.

The strongest evidence would connect deployment and production to the same workers and households, their full resources, prices and expenditure. Task and firm studies observe particular parts of that chain: assistance, output, hiring or wages. items.title: When the buyer finds an answer
items.content_html:
When the buyer finds an answer

A buyer hesitates because a product description leaves a question unresolved. An answer can change whether the purchase happens. In that familiar situation, the useful service is more than a cheaper way to process a transaction already certain to occur. It changes the possibility of the transaction itself.

This gives AI deployment an economic path different from saving minutes on an unchanged task. The distinction matters because sales, operating cost and the work needed to fulfil an order can move together. We need to follow that movement, rather than select a labour-saving story before observing what changed.

Seven retail experiments on whether buyers purchase more

The demand side need not remain a hypothetical destination for a production gain. Fang and coauthors' June 2026 paper examines seven randomised GenAI workflow experiments on one cross-border retail platform in 2023–24. They span service, matching, advertising and seller assistance. Sales effects range from no detectable effect to 16.3 percent against the workflow's existing practice. The gains operate mainly through more people buying, rather than bigger carts; returns and ratings do not deteriorate in the reported comparisons.

Annualising the four positive sales effects gives an estimated USD 4.6–5.2 in additional sales per consumer, assuming linear addition without workflow overlap or synergies. It is a calculation from short experimental periods, not a year of observed extra sales. The study does not observe the full capital, engineering, inference and organisational costs, so the sales estimate is not net return. These details leave a constructive result intact: particular deployed workflows changed purchases in a randomised comparison.

A transaction becomes possible

The mechanism has a different economic shape from an assistant completing the same support case faster. If a buyer finds a suitable item or gets an answer needed to decide, work can improve by resolving a transaction that otherwise would not happen. Demand and the useful service change together. The firm's next question is whether the extra transactions repay the deployment and change its need for support, fulfilment or other work. A labour-saving story is only one possible account.

The experiments do not isolate that explanation from persuasion, attention, trust or novelty. More purchases could follow clearer information, more compelling presentation or some combination of them. The difference matters to the product: a buyer finding a better match and a buyer being persuaded to act can produce the same immediate sales result while leaving different reasons to return. Conversion locates the observed change; understanding the service requires following the buyer beyond it.

The retailer and the economy

For the retailer, resolving that hesitation can create an additional sale. For the buyer, it might replace a purchase elsewhere or bring a future purchase forward. Lower search friction can improve the choice without increasing the buyer's total budget. Following the gain beyond the platform requires those alternatives to be observed, together with the additional work, hours, pay and income claims that the transactions create. The experiment establishes a local purchase response; tracing its wider destination is a further economic question.

A local purchase response is worth understanding in its own right. It can reveal an unresolved need that better information helps a buyer meet. Whether the response creates a lasting return depends on the complete operating process, including what additional transactions require. Whether it changes the buyer's room to live depends on income and prices beyond that purchase. Finding an answer can improve a transaction without answering every question about its economic destination.
